signatureWhy: Blockbuster has a state-by-state store table in nine annual filings (1999 and 2004-2009 captured) and a store count that peaked and collapsed. A map is the visual that only this page can have; the stock chart and stage series support it.

factFile.label: What it was
factFile.value: A global provider of rental and retail movie and game entertainment: stores, by-mail, kiosks and digital

factFile.label: Founded
factFile.value: First store opened in Dallas, Texas
factFile.note: The predecessor company, Blockbuster Entertainment Corporation, was incorporated in Delaware in 1982 (fn 1).

factFile.label: Peak
factFile.value: 9,094 stores worldwide, 5,803 of them in the United States

factFile.label: End
factFile.value: Filed for Chapter 11 on Sep 23, 2010; Dish said Blockbuster had ceased all material operations on Dec 31, 2013
factFile.note: "Last corporate stores closed by January 2014" on the page is supported by the AP report of Nov 6, 2013 (early January) and Dish's Dec 31, 2013 statement; the exact closing date of the last store is not given in any source found.

factFile.label: Bought by
factFile.value: DISH Network, for $320.6 million; the sale closed Apr 26, 2011
factFile.note: Dish's own release of Apr 6, 2011 put its winning bid at about $320 million and expected about $228 million in cash at closing.

factFile.label: Owns the name today
factFile.value: Blockbuster L.L.C., a Colorado company at 9601 S. Meridian Blvd., Englewood, which is also DISH's principal executive office; Dish described it in 2014 as its wholly-owned subsidiary
factFile.note: Replaces "Dish Network (EchoStar) holds the brand": EchoStar's FY2025 10-K does not mention Blockbuster (see gap). The torn-ticket logo registration was cancelled in Feb 2023 (fn 43).

factFile.label: What remains
factFile.value: One franchised store in Bend, Oregon, and a holding page at blockbuster.com
factFile.note: The store's own website (fn 31) blocks scripted access, so current operation is supported by Seattle Met (2024) and KTVZ (Feb 2023); see gap.

timelineAdd.text: Viacom offers its shareholders 5.15 Blockbuster shares for each Viacom share. The exchange is oversubscribed, so Viacom accepts 9.55% of the shares tendered and swaps 27,961,165 of its own shares for 72 million each of Blockbuster Class A and Class B.
Class A shares trade ex-dividend for the $5.00 special distribution. The quarter's trading range runs from $15.12 to $7.24.
Blockbuster makes public a cash offer of at least $6.00 a share for Circuit City, sent in a letter on February 17, subject to due diligence.
Blockbuster sells $675 million of 11.75% senior secured notes.
Carl Icahn resigns from the board.
The shares leave the NYSE and trade on the Pink OTCQB market as BLOAQ and BLOBQ.
Dish says its winning bid is valued at about $320 million and that it expects to pay about $228 million in cash; it describes Blockbuster as having more than 1,700 store locations.
The company reports it has paid its senior secured lenders $100 million from the sale and expects to pay $24.6 million more, and says creditors will receive substantially less than payment in full.
Dish says Blockbuster operates over 1,500 stores in the United States.
Dish closed about 700 domestic stores during 2012, leaving about 800, and announces about 300 more closings in January 2013.
Blockbuster's two UK operating subsidiaries enter administration; Dish records charges of about $46 million. The 91 remaining UK stores close on December 16, 2013.
Dish says Blockbuster has ceased all material operations.
Dish completes the sale of Blockbuster Mexico after a $19 million impairment.
The bankruptcy docket of BB Liquidating Inc., the former Blockbuster Inc., is terminated.
Oregon's Redmond and Sandy stores have closed since about December 2017, leaving Bend as the only Blockbuster in the contiguous 48 states; five stores remain in Alaska.

now.title: The BLOCKBUSTER mark
now.text: The USPTO shows two live registrations for the word mark, renewed in 2023 and 2019, owned by Blockbuster L.L.C. of Englewood, Colorado. The registration for the torn-ticket logo was cancelled in February 2023 because no Section 8 declaration was filed.

now.title: The estate
now.text: Blockbuster Inc.'s bankruptcy case, number 10-14997, is captioned BB Liquidating Inc., is listed as Chapter 7 with Robert L. Geltzer as trustee, and was terminated on June 29, 2017.

now.title: The name inside Dish
now.text: Dish used the name for Blockbuster@Home, a streaming offer for its subscribers, and EchoStar completed its acquisition of Dish on December 31, 2023. blockbuster.com showed the line "We are working on rewinding your movie." with a link to Sling TV on October 10, 2026.

now.title: The Bend store
now.text: At 211 NE Revere Ave #3, Bend, Oregon. It was Pacific Video until the 2000 franchise conversion, and became the only Blockbuster in the contiguous 48 states by March 2018 and the only one in the world in March 2019. In February 2023 it said movie rentals for locals were up about 200 percent and some mornings it filled 90 online orders.

now.title: The corporate stores
now.text: Dish operated over 1,500 stores at the end of 2011, about 800 at the end of 2012 and announced on November 6, 2013 that about 300 remaining stores would close by early January 2014, with about 2,800 jobs lost. The UK arm entered administration in January 2013; its last 91 stores closed on December 16, 2013. Mexico was sold on January 14, 2014.

now.title: The lenders
now.text: At the filing, $600.7 million of senior secured notes and $300.0 million of senior subordinated notes were outstanding. By July 12, 2011 the senior secured lenders had been paid $100 million from the sale, with $24.6 million more expected.

glossary.def: Blockbuster's term for a late fee: a charge when a rental was kept past its due date.
A one-time payment to shareholders outside the regular dividend.
A way for a parent company to give up a subsidiary by exchanging shareholders' parent shares for subsidiary shares.
A court-supervised sale of a bankrupt company's assets, usually through an auction, that passes the assets to the buyer free of most claims.
Bonds that are repaid after secured and senior debt if the company cannot pay everyone.
A loan made to a company in Chapter 11 that is repaid ahead of most older debts.
A deal in which a rental chain pays a studio a smaller up-front price and shares the rental income instead.

insights.summary: The notes issued in 2004 to pay the Viacom distribution were still on the books at the filing, and the sale could not cover the debt ahead of them. On Jan 2, 2011 liabilities subject to compromise included $300.0M of 9% senior subordinated notes (issued Aug 20, 2004, the same day as the $1,150M facility that funded the $905.6M distribution) behind $600.7M of senior secured notes (the company had sold $675M of 11.75% secured notes on Oct 1, 2009). The sale fetched $320.6M, less than the secured notes alone. The company said creditors would receive substantially less than payment in full and, by Jul 12, 2011, had paid its senior secured lenders $100M with $24.6M more expected. The sale price is a gross figure; the estate expected about $226M net.
insights.where: Cause: "Debt taken on to leave Viacom"; story chapter "Collapse"; numbers section as a recovery bar

insights.summary: Ending late fees cost more than the company projected. In its FY2004 10-K Blockbuster projected the fees would have contributed $400M to $450M of 2005 revenue and $250M to $300M of operating income. In the FY2005 10-K it said the "no late fees" program had cost about $60M to implement and reduced rental revenues by over $500M, and that extended viewing fees had been approximately 14% of 2004 rental revenues. By March 2006 about 340 franchise stores had followed.
insights.where: Story chapter "Independent, indebted and under new management"; numbers "What late fees were worth"

insights.summary: The store map shows no state gaining stores between Dec 2004 and Jan 2010. U.S. stores fell from 5,803 to 4,018 (-31%), but franchised stores fell faster (1,095 to 493, -55%) than company-operated ones (4,708 to 3,525, -25%). California lost the most (681 to 468) and Montana the largest share (8 to 1); New Mexico fell from 35 to 7 and Idaho from 16 to 4. Percentages and differences are derived from the two filing tables.
insights.where: Signature visual: store map, with a caption and a "biggest losses" list

insights.summary: Dish cut the U.S. chain from more than 1,700 locations at the April 2011 deal to over 1,500 at the end of 2011, about 800 at the end of 2012 (after about 700 closings) and about 300 when it announced the end in November 2013. It reported net losses from discontinued operations of $47M in 2013 and $37M in 2012. These are Dish's company-operated counts, not comparable to the earlier franchise-inclusive counts.

insights.summary: The chain Blockbuster tried to buy in 2005 was profitable. Hollywood Entertainment reported (as restated) net income of $71.3M on $1,782.4M of revenue in 2004, with $351.3M of long-term obligations. Blockbuster's own 2004 figures were a $1,248.8M net loss (mostly non-cash impairments) and $1,119.7M of long-term debt. Hollywood still ended up inside Movie Gallery, which entered bankruptcy in 2007; the profit did not save the model.
